questions.question: What histopathologic features on muscle biopsy distinguish immune‑mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM) from other inflammatory myopathies such as polymyositis and dermatomyositis?
A patient presents with progressive proximal weakness, dysphagia, CK > 3000 U/L, and normal ANA panel. Which sequence of laboratory and imaging studies is most appropriate to evaluate for IMNM?
Which autoantibodies are most strongly associated with immune‑mediated necrotising myopathy, and how does their presence—or absence—affect diagnostic confidence and therapeutic decisions?
When a patient on a GLP‑1 receptor agonist develops elevated CK, how can clinicians differentiate acute drug‑induced rhabdomyolysis from a drug‑triggered immune‑mediated necrotising myopathy?
According to WHO‑Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC) causality categories, what elements of this case satisfy the criteria for labeling semaglutide as a ‘probable’ cause of the patient’s IMNM?
Discuss plausible pathophysiologic mechanisms by which GLP‑1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide could precipitate an autoimmune muscle injury like IMNM.

In a patient with chronic NAFLD who now has markedly elevated AST/ALT alongside high CK, what clinical clues help determine whether transaminase elevation originates from liver injury versus skeletal muscle breakdown?
What is the recommended first‑line therapeutic regimen for seronegative IMNM, and why is intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) added to high‑dose corticosteroids in severe cases?

Given the patient’s mildly elevated troponin and cardiac MRI showing myocardial edema without late gadolinium enhancement, what cardiac complications should be screened for in IMNM, and what follow‑up strategy is appropriate?

In seronegative IMNM patients who achieve remission after a short course of steroids and IVIG with withdrawal of the offending agent, how long should clinicians continue surveillance for disease relapse, and which biomarkers or clinical assessments are most useful during follow‑up?
